stem: A static route is configured with only a next-hop address and no exit interface. How does the router decide which interface will carry the traffic?
explanation: The router performs a recursive lookup: it searches the routing table for a route covering the next-hop address and forwards out that route's interface. This is why the next hop must itself be reachable — if the recursion fails, the static route never enters the table.

choices.text: It performs a recursive lookup to find a route that covers the next-hop address
It ARPs for the next hop simultaneously on every up interface
It uses the lowest-numbered interface that is up and forwarding
It requires a default route to be present before the static route can install

stem: What is the drawback of a static route that specifies an exit interface but no next-hop address on a multi-access Ethernet segment?
explanation: Without a next hop, the router treats every destination inside the prefix as directly connected and issues a separate ARP for each one, instead of resolving a single next-hop MAC. That floods the segment with ARP traffic and consumes adjacency and memory resources as the prefix grows.

choices.text: The router must resolve a MAC address for every destination, so it ARPs once per destination instead of once per next hop
The route is not installed until the interface receives a DHCP lease
The route is silently converted into a default route
The route inherits the administrative distance of the interface and is ignored

stem: Which keyword keeps a static route in the routing table even when its outgoing interface goes down?
explanation: The permanent keyword decouples the route from interface state, so it stays installed regardless. It is used where the interface flaps for reasons unrelated to path availability — dial backup links and some floating static designs — and it means the route will attract traffic that cannot actually be delivered.

choices.text: permanent
track
sticky
persist

stem: How does a static route behave differently from a dynamically learned route when the topology changes?
explanation: Nothing recalculates a static route. It remains exactly as configured until an administrator changes or removes it, which is both its strength (predictable, no protocol overhead) and its weakness (no automatic reaction to a failed path).

choices.text: It does not react at all; it stays configured and must be changed manually
It reconverges faster because it has no protocol timers
It is withdrawn automatically as soon as any link fails
It is recalculated by the SPF algorithm like any other route

stem: In a router-on-a-stick design, how must the switch port facing the router be configured?
explanation: The router needs to see the 802.1Q tag for each VLAN, and an access port would strip or reject those tags. The link must therefore be a trunk carrying every VLAN that the router is expected to route between.

choices.text: As an 802.1Q trunk carrying every VLAN that needs routing
As an access port in the native VLAN
As a routed port with an IP address in each VLAN
As an access port in VLAN 1, because VLAN 1 carries all VLANs

stem: Which interface command converts a switch port into a Layer 3 routed port so that an IP address can be assigned directly to it?
explanation: no switchport removes the port from Layer 2 switching and makes it a routed interface, after which ip address applies normally. This is how a multilayer switch builds a point-to-point link toward a router or another L3 switch without consuming a VLAN.

choices.text: no switchport
switchport mode trunk
no ip address
encapsulation dot1q native

stem: Which command configures subinterface GigabitEthernet0/0.30 to carry VLAN 30 as the native VLAN while still applying 802.1Q encapsulation?
explanation: The native keyword tells the router that frames for this VLAN arrive untagged, matching the switch's native VLAN setting. Without it the router would expect a tag on those frames and drop them.

choices.text: encapsulation dot1Q 30 native
encapsulation dot1Q 30
switchport trunk native vlan 30
encapsulation native 30

stem: A multilayer switch has both its VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 interfaces up/up, yet hosts in VLAN 10 cannot reach hosts in VLAN 20. Which global command is missing?
explanation: SVIs exist and are up, but a multilayer switch forwards only at Layer 2 until routing is enabled globally. ip routing turns on the Layer 3 forwarding path between SVIs. It is a global command, not a per-interface one, which is why both SVIs look healthy while traffic still fails.

choices.text: ip routing
ip routing enable
ipv6 unicast-routing
switchport routing

stem: What does route poisoning do when a network becomes unreachable?
explanation: Instead of removing the route and saying nothing, the router advertises it with an infinite metric. Neighbors immediately mark the path unusable instead of continuing to believe their own stale entry, which is what prevents a routing loop while the failure propagates.

choices.text: It advertises the failed network with an infinite metric so neighbors stop using that path
It deletes the route locally without telling any neighbor
It re-advertises the failed prefix with a metric of zero
It keeps advertising the old metric until the hold-down timer expires

stem: Why can a distance-vector protocol count to infinity after a link fails?
explanation: When A loses a directly connected network, B may still advertise a route to it back to A. A accepts B's advertisement, then B accepts A's new advertisement, and the metric climbs one hop at a time. Split horizon, route poisoning, and triggered updates exist precisely to break that mutual belief.

choices.text: Neighbors keep believing each other's stale advertisements, so the metric increases one hop at a time
The hop-count field overflows and wraps back to zero
The update timer expires and duplicates every route in the table
The topology table loses its successor and floods a query to every neighbor

stem: What is the fundamental difference between a link-state and a distance-vector routing protocol?
explanation: A link-state protocol floods link information so every router builds an identical topology database and independently runs SPF. A distance-vector protocol never sees the topology — it only knows which neighbor offers the best metric to a prefix and trusts that neighbor.

choices.text: Link-state builds a full topology database and runs SPF; distance-vector only knows routes and metrics learned from neighbors
Link-state uses hop count as its metric; distance-vector uses bandwidth
Link-state protocols are classful; distance-vector protocols are classless
Link-state sends its full table every 30 seconds; distance-vector exchanges LSAs

stem: What is the purpose of the hold-down timer in a distance-vector routing protocol?
explanation: After a route is declared unreachable, the hold-down period suppresses it so a flapping interface or a stale, pre-failure update cannot put the route back into service immediately. The cost is slower reconvergence for a path that recovers quickly.

choices.text: It suppresses a recently failed route so flapping or stale updates cannot reinstate it immediately
It delays hello packets so the CPU is not interrupted too often
It limits how long a router waits for an acknowledgement from a neighbor
It ages out table entries that have not changed

stem: Which single prefix summarizes the contiguous networks 10.0.0.0/24, 10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24, and 10.0.3.0/24?
explanation: Four /24 networks align on a four-block boundary, so two bits of prefix are removed: 24 - 2 = 22. The result 10.0.0.0/22 covers exactly 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.3.255 with nothing left over.

stem: Why is it unsafe to summarize 172.16.1.0/24 and 172.16.3.0/24 as 172.16.0.0/22?
explanation: The /22 spans four /24 blocks, and two of them — 172.16.0.0/24 and 172.16.2.0/24 — are not part of the pair being summarized. Advertising the /22 pulls traffic for those two networks toward the summarizer, which then has no route and drops it.

choices.text: The /22 also covers 172.16.0.0/24 and 172.16.2.0/24, so traffic for those networks is drawn in and dropped
A summary must always be a /24 or longer to be advertised
RFC 1918 space cannot be summarized at all
The two subnets use different administrative distances

stem: Which command configures manual inter-area summarization of 10.1.0.0/16 on an OSPF ABR inside area 1?
explanation: The area range command on an ABR collapses matching intra-area prefixes into a single Type 3 LSA for the other areas. The similar-looking summary-address command is different: it summarizes redistributed external prefixes into Type 5 LSAs on an ASBR.

choices.text: summary-address 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0
area 1 range 10.1.0.0/16

stem: Why is 0.0.0.0/0 described as the ultimate summary?
explanation: A /0 removes every prefix bit, so the prefix covers the entire IPv4 address space. As a route it therefore matches any destination that no more specific entry matches, which is exactly what a default route does.

choices.text: It covers every IPv4 address, so it matches anything no more specific prefix covers
It summarizes only the RFC 1918 private ranges
It is the shortest prefix a router is allowed to store
It is generated automatically by every routing protocol

stem: A floating static route must back up an eBGP-learned route. Which administrative distance keeps the static route out of the table while eBGP is healthy?
explanation: eBGP is installed with an administrative distance of 20, so the static route needs any value above 20 to lose the comparison. Choosing a value above 200 would still work but would also lose to iBGP, which is a different design intent.

choices.text: Any value greater than 20
Any value greater than 90
Any value greater than 110
Exactly 255

stem: What happens to a static route configured with an administrative distance of 255?
explanation: 255 is the maximum value and reserves the route from ever being installed, because it can never win against any other source. It is a way of writing a route down without activating it, and routes that fail reachability checks appear with this AD in show output.

choices.text: It is never installed in the routing table, no matter what other routes exist
It becomes the last-resort gateway
It is installed but immediately marked unreachable
It is installed only while the outgoing interface is down

stem: Which pair of commands makes a floating static route depend on the result of an IP SLA probe?
explanation: The tracked object is defined first, then attached to the route with the track keyword. If the probe fails, the object goes down and the router withdraws the static route even though the local interface is still up — which is the only way to detect a failure that happens beyond the first hop.

choices.text: track 1 ip sla 1, then ip route 10.2.2.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.2 250 track 1
ip sla 1, then ip route 10.2.2.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.2 250 permanent
track 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 line-protocol, then ip route 10.2.2.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.2 250
ip sla monitor 1, then ip route 10.2.2.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.2 250 name SLA

stem: Two static routes reach the same destination: one with AD 200 via ISP-A and one with AD 210 via ISP-B. Both next hops are reachable. What does the router do?
explanation: Only the lowest administrative distance is installed, so the AD 200 route owns the destination and the AD 210 route stays out of the routing table entirely. It is not a standby in the table — it becomes usable only when the AD 200 route disappears.

choices.text: It installs only the AD 200 route; the AD 210 route is used only if the first one disappears
It installs both routes and load-balances across the two ISPs
It installs neither route because their administrative distances disagree
It installs the AD 210 route because a higher distance is preferred

stem: Which command displays the IPv6 routing table on a Cisco router?
explanation: IPv6 has its own table, separate from the IPv4 table, and show ipv6 route prints it. The output uses the same route codes — C, L, S, O, D — so the IPv4 reading skills transfer directly.

choices.text: show ipv6 route
show ip route v6
show route ipv6
show ipv6 routing-table

stem: Which command creates an IPv6 static route for 2001:db8:2::/48 out GigabitEthernet0/1 with link-local next hop fe80::1?
explanation: A link-local next hop is only unique on a single link, so the exit interface must be given alongside it. The keyword form is interface first, then address. Omitting the interface makes the next hop ambiguous and the router rejects the route.

choices.text: ipv6 route 2001:db8:2::/48 GigabitEthernet0/1 fe80::1
ip route 2001:db8:2::/48 GigabitEthernet0/1 fe80::1
ipv6 route 2001:db8:2:: 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/1 fe80::1

stem: A static IPv6 route is pointed at the Null0 interface. What is that route used for?
explanation: Null0 silently discards anything sent to it, so a route to Null0 black-holes a prefix. The usual reason is to drop traffic for the unused part of a summarized range, preventing the router from following a less specific route and looping those packets.

choices.text: It silently discards matching traffic, which is used to black-hole unused space inside a summary
It returns an ICMP error to the source for every matching packet
It forwards matching traffic to the default gateway instead
It logs matching packets and then forwards them normally

stem: Why is an IPv6 static route with only an exit interface and no next hop acceptable on a point-to-point link but not on a shared Ethernet segment?
explanation: On a point-to-point link there is exactly one possible neighbor, so the router can send toward the far end without choosing between candidates. On a multi-access segment there are many neighbors, so the router would have to resolve a link-layer address for each destination and treat the whole prefix as directly attached.

choices.text: Only one neighbor can exist on a point-to-point link, so the far end is unambiguous
Point-to-point links do not use link-local addresses
The interface supplies a synthetic next-hop address automatically
The router converts the route into a connected route on point-to-point links

stem: What is the default administrative distance of a static route?
explanation: A static route is trusted almost completely — only a directly connected route, at 0, beats it. That is why a mistyped static route can silently override a routing protocol that would have chosen a working path.

stem: What is the default administrative distance of an EIGRP route learned from outside the local EIGRP autonomous system?
explanation: Internal EIGRP is 90 because the whole path is inside one administrative domain. An external route originated elsewhere is only as trustworthy as the protocol it came from, so EIGRP assigns it 170 — worse than OSPF, better than RIP.

stem: An administrator sets a static route's administrative distance to 5 on Router A, and Router A then redistributes that route into OSPF. What administrative distance do Router A's OSPF neighbors assign to the route?
explanation: Administrative distance is purely local. It expresses how much this router trusts a source and is never encoded in a routing update, so neighbors evaluate the route as an OSPF route and apply OSPF's own distance of 110.

choices.text: 110, because administrative distance is local and is never carried in routing updates
5, because the original value travels with the route
20, because redistributed routes become external
0, because the value is reset at every hop

stem: Which statement correctly compares HSRP and VRRP?
explanation: VRRP is defined in an RFC and works between vendors, so it is the choice in mixed environments. HSRP is Cisco-developed and, while widely deployed in all-Cisco networks, does not interoperate with other vendors' first-hop redundancy implementations.

choices.text: VRRP is an open standard, while HSRP is Cisco-proprietary
HSRP is an open standard, while VRRP is Cisco-proprietary
Both are open standards maintained by the IETF
Both are Cisco-proprietary and interoperate only with each other

stem: Which virtual MAC address format does HSRP version 2 use?
explanation: HSRPv1 uses 0000.0c07.acXX, which caps the group number at 255. Version 2 moved to 0000.0c9f.fXXX and encodes the group in the low 10 bits, allowing group numbers far beyond 255.

choices.text: 0000.0c9f.fXXX

stem: What are the default hello and hold timers for HSRP version 1?
explanation: HSRPv1 sends a hello every 3 seconds and declares the peer dead after 10 seconds without one. The hold time is roughly three hellos, so a single lost packet does not trigger a failover, and both timers must match across the group for it to work.

choices.text: 3 seconds hello, 10 seconds hold
1 second hello, 3 seconds hold
5 seconds hello, 15 seconds hold
10 seconds hello, 30 seconds hold
